The Datalabs Agency designs dashboards people actually use every day, built as working tools people rely on, not boardroom decoration. Since 2012 we have designed dashboards and BI style guides for clients including Mercedes-Benz, Adidas, and UPS, in whichever platform your data already lives in.

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][dfd_delimiter delimiter_style="dfd-delimiter-with-icon" icon_size="30" delimiter_border_style="dotted" icon_fontawesome="fa fa-solid fa-circle-arrow-down" show_icon="enable_icon" delim_line_color="#8224E31C" icon_color="#EEE6F6" icon_hover_color="#D4C9E0"][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="35" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="35" screen_tablet_spacer_size="35" screen_mobile_spacer_size="35"][vc_single_image image="52827" img_size="large" alignment="center" css=""][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="35" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="35" screen_tablet_spacer_size="35" screen_mobile_spacer_size="35"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" heading_margin="margin-bottom:20px;" subtitle="The short version" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_size:70|line_height:64" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_size:38|line_height:32"]

What does a dashboard design service actually do?

[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

A dashboard design service turns disconnected reports into one dashboard people actually read — the right chart types for the data, a clear visual hierarchy, and a layout built around the decisions your team makes every week with it.

The Datalabs Agency is a Melbourne-based data visualization consultancy founded in 2012 that delivers corporate training workshops (Power BI, Tableau, data storytelling), dashboard design, and BI style guides for clients including Mercedes-Benz, Adidas, and UPS.

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="80" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="80" screen_tablet_spacer_size="80" screen_mobile_spacer_size="80"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" heading_margin="margin-bottom:20px;" subtitle="Not locked to one platform" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_size:70|line_height:64" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_size:38|line_height:32"]

Do you only design Power BI dashboards?

[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

No. We design dashboards in Power BI, Tableau, Excel, and PowerPoint, and the design work — layout, hierarchy, colour, chart choice — comes first regardless of the platform. If you specifically want a build-out inside one tool, we have a dedicated page for it.

Design and software are two different jobs, and treating them as one is a common reason corporate dashboards are technically correct and still hard to read. Our process starts with the question the dashboard has to answer, then chooses the chart types, layout, and colour system that answer it fastest — the platform gets picked to fit the data, never the reverse. Power BI and Tableau are common enough on their own to deserve dedicated pages: see our Power BI dashboard design page for a build inside that platform, or our Tableau dashboard design page for a Tableau-specific project. This page covers the design service more broadly, across whatever tool your data already lives in.

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="60" screen_tablet_spacer_size="60" screen_mobile_spacer_size="60"][dfd_button button_text="Get a project quote" buttom_link_src="url:https%3A%2F%2Fwww.datalabsagency.com%2Fcontact-us%2F|||" style="style_6" background="#8a8f6a" hover_background="#4e5041" border="border-style:none;|border-radius:5px;" hover_border="border-style:none;|border-radius:5px;"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner el_class="dfd_col-tablet-12" width="1/4" offset="vc_col-lg-3 vc_col-md-2 vc_col-xs-1"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="40" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][/vc_column][/vc_row] [vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay="" el_id="pat-faq"][vc_column width="1/4"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/2"][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="40" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][vc_column_text css="" item_animation="transition.fadeIn"]

Questions & Answers

Dashboard design services

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="30" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][dfd_accordion style="style-3" active_section="1" font_size="18" tab_title_google_fonts="yes" tab_title_custom_fonts="font_family:Arvo%3Aregular%2Citalic%2C700%2C700italic|font_style:700%20bold%20regular%3A700%3Anormal" icon_size="14"][vc_tta_section title="How much does dashboard design cost?" tab_id="1685677784578-172f9372-59216fce-87a69a68-2eae"][vc_column_text css=""]

It depends on how many dashboards you need and how much of your own data and branding is involved, so every project is scoped individually rather than priced off a flat rate card. As a reference point, our published data visualisation consulting rate is $250 per hour (1-hour blocks, up to 4 hours), and workshop-based dashboard training runs $3,000 to $8,000 per workshop day. Send us your brief through the contact form and we will reply with a fixed quote.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Which BI tools do you design dashboards for?" tab_id="1685677784323-438be9dd-da0e6fce-87a69a68-2eae"][vc_column_text css=""]

Power BI, Tableau, Excel, and PowerPoint are all in scope, and the design process is the same across every one of them. If you specifically want a Power BI dashboard design rebuild or a Tableau dashboard design project, those pages go deeper on the platform-specific detail.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="What is the difference between this and the dashboard workshop?" tab_id="1685677784395-526dd6ff-b9c26fce-87a69a68-2eae"][vc_column_text css=""]

This service is done for you: our team designs the dashboard and hands it over finished. The Designing Great Dashboards workshop teaches your own team to design dashboards themselves, which suits a team that wants the skill in-house. Some clients book both, training first and a design pass second.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="How long does a dashboard design project take?" tab_id="1685677784507-83427dcb-7a756fce-87a69a68-2eae"][vc_column_text css=""]

Timing depends on how many dashboards you need and how many data sources and stakeholder reviews are involved, so we give you a real timeline once we understand the brief rather than a generic estimate that will not match your project. Ask for a timeline alongside your quote and you will get both together.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Do you provide an ongoing style guide, or just the one dashboard?" tab_id="1786584255290-781b75e9-21a0"][vc_column_text css=""]

Both are available. A single dashboard design project is scoped as its own piece of work, and many clients pair it with a data visualisation style guide — a shared reference for colour, typography, and chart conventions so every dashboard built afterwards, by us or by your own team, looks like it belongs to the same business.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Do you work with teams outside Australia?" tab_id="1788000000006-dashboard-design-q6"][vc_column_text css=""]

Yes. Based in Melbourne, we work with clients across Australia, the United States, Europe, and the Middle East, with design projects run remotely and reviewed over video calls at whatever cadence suits your team.

What happens in a dashboard design project?

[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

We start with your existing reports and data sources, then design the visual hierarchy — what to show first, what to group, what to drop — before touching colour or chart type. You review working wireframes, then get a finished dashboard built in your platform of choice.

Consistency matters as much as any single dashboard, especially once a team has more than one. That is why many design projects also produce a BI style guide — a shared reference for colour, typography, and chart conventions, so every dashboard built afterwards looks consistent instead of carrying five different analysts’ personal taste.

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][/vc_column][/vc_row] [vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" dfd_enable_overlay="" dfd_row_config="full_width_content_paddings" el_id="pat-section-2"][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="40" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/2"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" heading_margin="margin-bottom:20px;" subtitle="What actually goes wrong" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_size:70|line_height:64" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_size:38|line_height:32"]

Why do so many dashboards go unused?

[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

Most unused dashboards were built starting from whichever data was easiest to pull rather than the decision someone needed to make. Too many metrics on one screen, no visual hierarchy, and no consistent colour or chart system across the business are the three patterns we see most often in the audits we run before a redesign.

It comes down to communication design more than software. Most teams go straight to the software and treat the layout as whatever the tool defaults to; deciding what the reader sees first, and cutting everything that does not change a decision, is the part a specialist design pass adds — the same underlying data, arranged so someone can read it and act on it in under a minute.

[/vc_column_text][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/4"][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="40" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="40" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][/vc_column][/vc_row] [vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" css=".vc_custom_1691550358421{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}" el_id="pat-article-1"][vc_column width="1/6"][/vc_column][vc_column width="4/6"][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="60" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="40" screen_tablet_spacer_size="30" screen_mobile_spacer_size="40"][dfd_heading enable_delimiter="" style="style_02" heading_margin="margin-bottom:20px;" subtitle="The three failure patterns" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_size:70|line_height:64" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3|font_size:38|line_height:32"]

Why most dashboards go unread

[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="15" screen_mobile_spacer_size="19"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/2"][vc_column_text]

Most dashboards fail for the same reason a badly organised report fails: someone spent all their effort assembling the numbers and none of it deciding what the reader should notice first. We see this pattern constantly — a dashboard carrying every metric the business tracks on one screen, no visual hierarchy, and no quick way to tell whether last week was good or bad.

The fix is rarely more data or a fancier chart library. It is design — deciding what matters most, placing it where the eye lands first, and cutting whatever does not change a decision. We work through three questions before a single chart gets drawn: what decision does this dashboard support, who is making it, and how often will they actually look at it.

Consistency compounds the problem across a team. One analyst designs in blue and green, the next reuses the company brand palette, a third keeps whatever the software defaulted to, and within a year the business has a dozen dashboards that look like they came from a dozen different companies. That is why many of our design projects also produce a BI style guide — the same colour system, chart types, and layout conventions applied to everything built afterwards, well beyond the one dashboard we design directly.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/2"][vc_column_text]

We have designed dashboards and BI style guides since 2012 for clients including Mercedes-Benz, Adidas, and UPS. Our founder learned visual storytelling at National Geographic before bringing it to corporate dashboards, and that shows up in a specific way: we design for the person reading the dashboard under time pressure, not the analyst who already knows the data by heart.

None of this requires switching tools. The same design work happens in whatever platform your data already lives in — Power BI, Tableau, Excel, or PowerPoint — because the design decisions come first and the software is simply where they get built.

Templates, training, or a design service — which fits?

[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="20" screen_mobile_spacer_size="20"][vc_column_text css=""]

The right approach depends on whether your team needs one dashboard, an in-house skill, or both.

CriterionTemplatesTeam workshopDesign service
Who builds itYou, from a templateYour team, taught liveThe Datalabs Agency
Built around your own data—✓✓
Ongoing skill stays in-house—✓—

Templates and the design service are not exclusive — many clients start with the workshop to build in-house skill, then commission a design pass to raise the bar on the dashboards that matter most.

How a dashboard design project runs

[/dfd_heading][dfd_spacer screen_wide_resolution="1280" screen_wide_spacer_size="20" screen_normal_resolution="1024" screen_tablet_resolution="800" screen_mobile_resolution="480" screen_normal_spacer_size="20" screen_tablet_spacer_size="15" screen_mobile_spacer_size="19"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/2"][vc_column_text]

Every project starts with the reports and data your team already has instead of a blank page. We review what exists, talk to the people who will actually use the finished dashboard, and work out what decision it needs to support — that single question shapes almost every design choice that follows.

From there we design the visual hierarchy before we touch colour or chart type: what the reader sees first, what gets grouped together, and what gets cut entirely. Everything crammed onto one screen is usually a sign nobody made that call deliberately, so we make it on purpose and show it to you as a wireframe before any of it gets built.

Once the layout is signed off, we build the finished dashboard in your platform — Power BI, Tableau, Excel, or PowerPoint — applying one consistent colour and chart system across it, instead of each screen carrying its own improvised choices. Teams that want that consistency to extend beyond a single dashboard usually add a BI style guide to the project, so the next dashboard someone on your team builds follows the same rules automatically.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/2"][vc_column_text]

We also run this the other way around. Teams that want the skill in-house start with our Designing Great Dashboards workshop instead, then bring us in for a design pass once they have built a few dashboards themselves and know where the gaps sit. Both paths end at the same place — dashboards people actually read — they simply start from different points.

A finished project includes the working dashboard file, source assets, and a short handover walkthrough with whoever on your team maintains it, so you are not dependent on us for small changes afterwards. If your data changes shape later or a new source gets added, that is ordinary maintenance — a separate conversation from the original design.

[vc_column_text css=””]

The Datalabs Agency designs dashboards people actually use every day, built as working tools people rely on, not boardroom decoration. Since 2012 we have designed dashboards and BI style guides for clients including Mercedes-Benz, Adidas, and UPS, in whichever platform your data already lives in.

[/vc_column_text]
[vc_single_image image=”52827″ img_size=”large” alignment=”center” css=””]

The short version

What does a dashboard design service actually do?

[vc_column_text css=””]

A dashboard design service turns disconnected reports into one dashboard people actually read — the right chart types for the data, a clear visual hierarchy, and a layout built around the decisions your team makes every week with it.

The Datalabs Agency is a Melbourne-based data visualization consultancy founded in 2012 that delivers corporate training workshops (Power BI, Tableau, data storytelling), dashboard design, and BI style guides for clients including Mercedes-Benz, Adidas, and UPS.

[/vc_column_text]

Not locked to one platform

Do you only design Power BI dashboards?

[vc_column_text css=””]

No. We design dashboards in Power BI, Tableau, Excel, and PowerPoint, and the design work — layout, hierarchy, colour, chart choice — comes first regardless of the platform. If you specifically want a build-out inside one tool, we have a dedicated page for it.

Design and software are two different jobs, and treating them as one is a common reason corporate dashboards are technically correct and still hard to read. Our process starts with the question the dashboard has to answer, then chooses the chart types, layout, and colour system that answer it fastest — the platform gets picked to fit the data, never the reverse. Power BI and Tableau are common enough on their own to deserve dedicated pages: see our Power BI dashboard design page for a build inside that platform, or our Tableau dashboard design page for a Tableau-specific project. This page covers the design service more broadly, across whatever tool your data already lives in.

[/vc_column_text]

Questions & Answers

Dashboard design services

[/vc_column_text]
[dfd_accordion style=”style-3″ active_section=”1″ font_size=”18″ tab_title_google_fonts=”yes” tab_title_custom_fonts=”font_family:Arvo%3Aregular%2Citalic%2C700%2C700italic|font_style:700%20bold%20regular%3A700%3Anormal” icon_size=”14″][vc_tta_section title=”How much does dashboard design cost?” tab_id=”1685677784578-172f9372-59216fce-87a69a68-2eae”][vc_column_text css=””]

It depends on how many dashboards you need and how much of your own data and branding is involved, so every project is scoped individually rather than priced off a flat rate card. As a reference point, our published data visualisation consulting rate is $250 per hour (1-hour blocks, up to 4 hours), and workshop-based dashboard training runs $3,000 to $8,000 per workshop day. Send us your brief through the contact form and we will reply with a fixed quote.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”Which BI tools do you design dashboards for?” tab_id=”1685677784323-438be9dd-da0e6fce-87a69a68-2eae”][vc_column_text css=””]

Power BI, Tableau, Excel, and PowerPoint are all in scope, and the design process is the same across every one of them. If you specifically want a Power BI dashboard design rebuild or a Tableau dashboard design project, those pages go deeper on the platform-specific detail.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”What is the difference between this and the dashboard workshop?” tab_id=”1685677784395-526dd6ff-b9c26fce-87a69a68-2eae”][vc_column_text css=””]

This service is done for you: our team designs the dashboard and hands it over finished. The Designing Great Dashboards workshop teaches your own team to design dashboards themselves, which suits a team that wants the skill in-house. Some clients book both, training first and a design pass second.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”How long does a dashboard design project take?” tab_id=”1685677784507-83427dcb-7a756fce-87a69a68-2eae”][vc_column_text css=””]

Timing depends on how many dashboards you need and how many data sources and stakeholder reviews are involved, so we give you a real timeline once we understand the brief rather than a generic estimate that will not match your project. Ask for a timeline alongside your quote and you will get both together.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”Do you provide an ongoing style guide, or just the one dashboard?” tab_id=”1786584255290-781b75e9-21a0″][vc_column_text css=””]

Both are available. A single dashboard design project is scoped as its own piece of work, and many clients pair it with a data visualisation style guide — a shared reference for colour, typography, and chart conventions so every dashboard built afterwards, by us or by your own team, looks like it belongs to the same business.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”Do you work with teams outside Australia?” tab_id=”1788000000006-dashboard-design-q6″][vc_column_text css=””]

Yes. Based in Melbourne, we work with clients across Australia, the United States, Europe, and the Middle East, with design projects run remotely and reviewed over video calls at whatever cadence suits your team.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][/dfd_accordion][vc_raw_html][/vc_raw_html]

Wireframes before colour

What happens in a dashboard design project?

[vc_column_text css=””]

We start with your existing reports and data sources, then design the visual hierarchy — what to show first, what to group, what to drop — before touching colour or chart type. You review working wireframes, then get a finished dashboard built in your platform of choice.

Consistency matters as much as any single dashboard, especially once a team has more than one. That is why many design projects also produce a BI style guide — a shared reference for colour, typography, and chart conventions, so every dashboard built afterwards looks consistent instead of carrying five different analysts’ personal taste.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column]
[/vc_column][/vc_row] [vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” dfd_enable_overlay=”” dfd_row_config=”full_width_content_paddings” el_id=”pat-section-2″][vc_column]
[vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/2″]

What actually goes wrong

Why do so many dashboards go unused?

[vc_column_text css=””]

Most unused dashboards were built starting from whichever data was easiest to pull rather than the decision someone needed to make. Too many metrics on one screen, no visual hierarchy, and no consistent colour or chart system across the business are the three patterns we see most often in the audits we run before a redesign.

It comes down to communication design more than software. Most teams go straight to the software and treat the layout as whatever the tool defaults to; deciding what the reader sees first, and cutting everything that does not change a decision, is the part a specialist design pass adds — the same underlying data, arranged so someone can read it and act on it in under a minute.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/4″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column]
[/vc_column][/vc_row] [vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1691550358421{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}” el_id=”pat-article-1″][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”4/6″]

The three failure patterns

Why most dashboards go unread

[vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/2″][vc_column_text]

Most dashboards fail for the same reason a badly organised report fails: someone spent all their effort assembling the numbers and none of it deciding what the reader should notice first. We see this pattern constantly — a dashboard carrying every metric the business tracks on one screen, no visual hierarchy, and no quick way to tell whether last week was good or bad.

The fix is rarely more data or a fancier chart library. It is design — deciding what matters most, placing it where the eye lands first, and cutting whatever does not change a decision. We work through three questions before a single chart gets drawn: what decision does this dashboard support, who is making it, and how often will they actually look at it.

Consistency compounds the problem across a team. One analyst designs in blue and green, the next reuses the company brand palette, a third keeps whatever the software defaulted to, and within a year the business has a dozen dashboards that look like they came from a dozen different companies. That is why many of our design projects also produce a BI style guide — the same colour system, chart types, and layout conventions applied to everything built afterwards, well beyond the one dashboard we design directly.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/2″][vc_column_text]

We have designed dashboards and BI style guides since 2012 for clients including Mercedes-Benz, Adidas, and UPS. Our founder learned visual storytelling at National Geographic before bringing it to corporate dashboards, and that shows up in a specific way: we design for the person reading the dashboard under time pressure, not the analyst who already knows the data by heart.

None of this requires switching tools. The same design work happens in whatever platform your data already lives in — Power BI, Tableau, Excel, or PowerPoint — because the design decisions come first and the software is simply where they get built.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner]

Three ways to get there

Templates, training, or a design service — which fits?

[vc_column_text css=””]

The right approach depends on whether your team needs one dashboard, an in-house skill, or both.

Criterion Templates Team workshop Design service
Who builds it You, from a template Your team, taught live The Datalabs Agency
Built around your own data — ✓ ✓
Ongoing skill stays in-house — ✓ —
Best for A single simple dashboard Teams who want the skill long-term Dashboards that need to be right, on a deadline

Templates and the design service are not exclusive — many clients start with the workshop to build in-house skill, then commission a design pass to raise the bar on the dashboards that matter most.

[/vc_column_text]

[/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/6″][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][/vc_column][vc_column]
[/vc_column][/vc_row] [vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1691550358421{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}” el_id=”pat-article-2″][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”4/6″]

Stage by stage…

How a dashboard design project runs

[vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/2″][vc_column_text]

Every project starts with the reports and data your team already has instead of a blank page. We review what exists, talk to the people who will actually use the finished dashboard, and work out what decision it needs to support — that single question shapes almost every design choice that follows.

From there we design the visual hierarchy before we touch colour or chart type: what the reader sees first, what gets grouped together, and what gets cut entirely. Everything crammed onto one screen is usually a sign nobody made that call deliberately, so we make it on purpose and show it to you as a wireframe before any of it gets built.

Once the layout is signed off, we build the finished dashboard in your platform — Power BI, Tableau, Excel, or PowerPoint — applying one consistent colour and chart system across it, instead of each screen carrying its own improvised choices. Teams that want that consistency to extend beyond a single dashboard usually add a BI style guide to the project, so the next dashboard someone on your team builds follows the same rules automatically.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/2″][vc_column_text]

We also run this the other way around. Teams that want the skill in-house start with our Designing Great Dashboards workshop instead, then bring us in for a design pass once they have built a few dashboards themselves and know where the gaps sit. Both paths end at the same place — dashboards people actually read — they simply start from different points.

A finished project includes the working dashboard file, source assets, and a short handover walkthrough with whoever on your team maintains it, so you are not dependent on us for small changes afterwards. If your data changes shape later or a new source gets added, that is ordinary maintenance — a separate conversation from the original design.
